newsitem.title: USA: Swiss envoy denies foreign pressure led to fund plan.
newsitem.headline: Swiss envoy denies foreign pressure led to fund plan.

text.p: The Swiss government acted swiftly on approving a plan to create a $5 billion humanitarian fund because it was a good idea and not because it wanted to blunt foreign criticism, Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti said on Wednesday.

Cotti, meeting with reporters at the start of a U.S. visit, said the possibility that the Clinton administration will issue a report strongly critical of Switzerland's wartime financial dealings with the Nazis played no role in the government's surprise decision to propose the fund.

The report being prepared by Stuart Eizenstat, currently undersecretary of Commerce for International Trade, is expected to be critical of the Swiss wartime role and of a 1946 treaty in which Switzerland agreed to give the allies $58 million to compensate for its handling of gold looted by the Nazis during the war. U.S. government documents say the Swiss handled more than $400 million in Nazi gold.
But Cotti said the 1946 Washington agreement was "a definitive settlement" and added, "We can't imagine the rediscussion of the agreement."

The foreign minister, who will meet Eizenstat and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright in Washinton on Friday, said initial public reaction has been favorable to creating the foundation to aid victims of genocide and human rights abuses.
He said he was confident it would pass a public referendum expected sometime after its final approval in parliament in 1998.
But Cotti refused to make any predictions, saying, "I am not a prophet ... Our political system gives to the people the last word. Our task is to try to influence the population in the right way."

He warned that criticism from aboard would be counter-productive. "If they (the Swiss) feel the judgment of other countries is not correct, then they will react ... (We) want to create a favorable climate for the vote."

He said the government acted quickly to propose the humanitarian fund after the Swiss Central Bank came up with a plan to finance it with interest payments coming from a donation of Swiss gold stocks.

Thomas Borer, the Swiss official handling the government's response to criticism of its wartime role, said the idea was just too good to pass up and it could prove to be as important to humanitarian causes as the Red Cross is now.

Cotti will meet World Jewish Congress president Edgar Bronfman in New York on Thursday to discuss the humanitarian fund and a separate fund already established to aid Holocaust victims. After the meeting the two men will attend a lunch with U.S. Jewish leaders and Swiss banking and government officials.
The WJC led a two-year campaign to get Switzerland to set up a fund for Holocaust victims, charging that Swiss banks profited from the war.

The foreign minister said he had no plans to meet Switzerland's chief critic in the U.S. Senate, New York Republican Alfonse D'Amato, on this visit, saying that it was "quite difficult to have a dialogue" with him at present.
